overview: The Orange Free State was a white-ruled republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Bloemfontein became its administrative centre, while the struggle over land drew Basotho and other African communities into conflict with the settler state. Its imported map interval also covers later British rule.

periods.title: Republic
periods.summary: The Bloemfontein Convention recognized the republic in 1854. British annexation was proclaimed in 1900, while the war continued until 1902.

periods.title: Orange River Colony
periods.summary: British colonial government preceded incorporation into the Union in 1910.

items.text: Britain recognized the new republic at the Bloemfontein Convention in 1854 without consulting African chiefdoms. The agreement did not settle the frontier with Moshoeshoe’s Basotho kingdom. Political recognition on paper therefore left fundamental disputes over who possessed the land.

The Free State’s expansion cost Basotho communities much fertile land. Conflict concerned fields, grazing and livestock, not an empty strip between two colored shapes. Basotho farming and political life continued beyond the republic’s borders and within the wider region.

The First Raadsaal began in 1849 as a school and also served as a church. In 1854 it became the republic’s assembly hall and offices. A building could host lessons, worship and government in succession: the rooms did not insist on just one career.

When the assembly moved to larger premises in 1856, the old building returned to schooling until 1877. Today it is restored as a museum. Its changing uses provide evidence for the institutions of a growing town without making its present display an untouched classroom.

Before a piped supply, Bloemfontein households and businesses relied on streams, fountains, wells, dams and boreholes. Water had to be carried in buckets. A drink, a wash and cooking a meal all began with somebody moving a heavy load.

Water shortages became critical in 1894. The Modder River scheme, approved in 1896, brought water to town in 1899 through pumping facilities and pipes around Naval Hill. This changed urban infrastructure, though the account does not show every home receiving equal service.

Freshford House, completed in 1897, preserves the setting of an affluent Bloemfontein household. Red brick walls, bay windows, a carved wooden veranda and cast-iron details show the materials and decorative choices of this home. Its comfort should not stand in for the lives of the town’s poorer residents.

Bloemfontein’s Wagon Museum holds ox wagons, transport wagons, a stagecoach, mule wagons and smaller carts. These different vehicles remind us that carrying freight and carrying passengers presented different problems. The collection also discusses transport used by Black people in the early twentieth century.

Earlier ox wagons could slow down with metal skidpans chained beneath their rear wheels. The wheels stopped turning while the shoes dragged along the ground. It was an effective answer to a very serious downhill question: how do you persuade a loaded wagon to stop?

A Dutch phrase from the 1893 pass law is “verblijf brief”, meaning “residential pass”. The law required Black location residents over sixteen, women as well as men, to carry one. This small writing sample came from paperwork that could determine whether somebody was arrested.

Contemporary newspapers reported police raids in Waaihoek, including arrests of residents without passes. One resident complained about officers entering houses and dragging out older women. These accounts restore African households to a city history too easily told only through presidents and public buildings.

The National Museum was founded in 1877 and opened in 1878. Its first honorary curator, Hugh Exton, sought public donations, and collections grew until the old Raadsaal needed extensions. Collecting natural and human history became another form of organized learning in the republic.

During the South African War, British scorched-earth operations destroyed farms, and camps imprisoned Boer families and Black civilians. Poor food, water and sanitation caused terrible suffering. The Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902 ended the war, after Britain had already proclaimed annexation in 1900.

ending.text: The independent republic was defeated in the war ending in 1902. Its territory became the Orange River Colony, which joined the Union of South Africa in 1910. The peoples and settlements continued; the map record’s 1914 endpoint does not extend republican independence to that date.
